First, you have to realize that root access and jailbreaking are two totally different things. Root access is a Linux/Unix term that is tantamount to running as an administrator. Jailbreaking is the process of opening a "backdoor" to allow non-authorized apps to be installed on an iDevices.

Apple doesn't like jailbreaking because they want to control the market on applications. Jailbreaking is a way of exploiting the OS in a way that "tricks" it into installing a non-Apple appstore, which will allow the user to install applications which aren't in the Appstore. They don't like this because they want a say in what can/will go on your iDevice at all times. This kind of control is a two-way street:

First, it assures that they make money one every single application on every single iDevice out there. If you've downloaded it from the Apple Appstore, they're making money off of it. Jailbreaking allows a user to install apps that Apple can't make money off of, and that's not Apple's end-goal.

Second, it controls the user experience, which can be a good or bad thing. It assures that apps work flawlessly within the OS, but it also hinders working apps that don't pass Apple's ridiculous standards. It stops users from "tweaking" their system with applications which can change the way the OS looks/works.

Android doesn't like giving users root access for two reasons:

First, and this is the most difficult to accept, most users don't know how to use it properly, and it can cause a LOT of damage. Imagine running your Windows computer in administrative mode at all times. Every app you run, good or bad, has access to every file or configuration you have... and can change anything, because you're running the app as an administrator. This is the problem with running as Root, and should be avoided unless completely necessary.

Second, a lot of device manufacturers put a LOT of money into the User Interface (UI), and don't want that money to go to waste when you change it out. Samsung has TouchWiz, HTC has SenseUI, LG has LGUI, and the list goes on and on... which is why every manufacturer's Android interface looks different, even though it's the "same" Android core. A TON of time, resources, and money goes into developing these UI's, and none of these manufacturers want you to just "throw them away."

Not to mention that the UI can "suggest" you use HTC's search engine instead of Google as your search engine... or comes pre-installed with Samsung's browser, instead of Firefox/Chrome, and Samsung can collect your browsing habits of people who are too lazy/dumb to change it out... or HTC comes with their proprietary dialer, which you won't change out, so they can "track" your calling habits... or whatever you can think of.

If it sounds like Android is better about this (from the first paragraph being controversial), it is. Apple does its best to squash any attempt to jailbreak iDevices, and that's why iDevices keep getting updates so fast. Google actually creates phones (such as the Nexus or GPE lines) which are fully-able to root. Yes, Google discourages you from rooting the device unless you know exactly what you're doing, but that's a far cry from hindering you from rooting your device.

When you hear about Android rooting being stopped, it's usually from the device manufacturers (Sony, Samsung, LG, etc) and not from Google.

I was under the impression that jailbreaking an ios device was literally breaking out of the jail (or container/sandbox) that the OS operates in, similar to a freeBSD jail, and not just opening a "back door". Is that not the case?

Yes and no. Usually, jailbreaking is a method of exploiting free variables to "crash" the system and make it boot into a kind of "safe mode." While in this safe mode, you get the chance to install one program... And this is usually Cydia.

Now, Cydia acts like an Appstore, so you can download and install anything you want through there.

This is advantageous when you want to install something that's either not in the Appstore, or was taken out of the Appstore. It also let's you install configuration managers which will allow you to change settings regular users can't get to (such as themes and icon packs).

So, no, technically all you're doing is sneaking Cydia into the iOS ecosystem. But, yes, because Cydia becomes a backdoor.
